title: Your own tools with MCP

story: Halfway through RH-1234, Nova wants to know one thing: should the "No projects yet" card also show for a filter with no results? Only Sean can answer. Nova has Bash, so it could try curl against Slack, but there is no Slack token on the VM, and we want it that way. It also wants to look up how the team names empty states, which is written in the R&D brain, our team's knowledge base, and the brain is not in the repo.

The built-in tools read files and run commands. They cannot ask a person in the right Slack thread, and they cannot search our brain. Those are jobs for our own code, which holds the right credentials outside the model's reach. The model needs a way to say "please run that function for me".
hook.question: How do I give the model a function of mine to call, and control exactly what it can send and get back?

read.h: The model calls a name, your code runs
p: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way for a program to offer tools to a model. Each tool has a name, a description, and an input schema that says which arguments it takes. The model reads the description, decides to call the tool, and sends arguments that match the schema. The program that offers the tools, an MCP server, runs the call and sends back the result. Many MCP servers are separate programs, such as a browser driver or a GitHub connector. The SDK also lets you build one inside your own process in a few lines.

tool() takes the four parts of a tool. The name is what the model calls. The description is the real interface: the model never sees your TypeScript, only this sentence, so it decides from these words whether the tool fits. The input schema is a zod shape, a plain object of zod fields, and the SDK checks every call against it before your function runs. The handler is your async function; it gets typed arguments and returns content blocks, usually one text block. createSdkMcpServer() puts tools together under a server name.

notes.text: A stand-in for the brain: two pages, so the lab needs no network.
The name the model calls. It becomes mcp__nova__kb_search once it sits on the server named nova.
The description is what the model reads to decide when to call. Write it for the model, not for people.
A zod shape, not z.object(). describe() adds a sentence the model sees next to the field.
isError: true marks a failed call, so the model treats the text as a problem, not as an odd answer.
Annotations are hints. readOnlyHint lets the SDK run this tool in parallel with other read-only tools.
An in-process MCP server. Nothing listens on a port; the SDK talks to it inside your program.

read.h: What the model sees, and the name it must be allowed under
p: You can look at your tool exactly the way a model client sees it, with no model at all. The MCP library has an in-memory transport, a pair of connected pipes, so a small script can connect a client to your server, list the tools and call one. The zod shape comes out as JSON Schema, the description comes out word for word, and a call with a wrong argument type is refused before your handler runs.

In a session you pass the server in mcpServers. The key you use there becomes the server part of every tool's full name, which follows the pattern mcp__<server>__<tool>. Under dontAsk that full name must be in allowedTools, or every call is refused like any other unapproved tool. You may also see a ToolSearch call before your tool runs: by default the SDK sends only the names of MCP tools first, and the model loads a tool's full schema when it needs it.

notes.text: The key, nova, is the server part of the tool's full name.
mcp__<server>__<tool>. Without this line dontAsk refuses the call.
Print each tool call, so you can see that the model really asked for kb_search.

p: A failing tool never crashes the session. If the arguments do not match the schema, the SDK refuses them and the model gets the validation error. If your handler throws, the in-process server catches it and the model gets the raw error message as a failed result. If your handler returns isError: true, the model gets exactly the text you wrote. In all three cases the model can try again, choose another tool or explain the problem, so the best error text says what to do next, for example "No page matches; try a shorter question".

Keep handlers small and boring. The schema already checked the input, so the handler calls one thing (for us, always the broker, the service that holds the real tokens), and returns text. Deciding what the answer means belongs to the model or to the harness, not to the tool. And because a handler is an ordinary function, you test it like one: call it with an input object and check content[0].text, with no session and no model.

deeper.h: Go deeper: servers that are separate programs
p: Some tools already exist as separate programs, such as the Playwright MCP server, which drives a browser. You add them to mcpServers with type "stdio", a command and its arguments, and the SDK starts the program as a child process and talks to it over standard input and output.

strictMcpConfig: true makes the session use only the servers in your options object, and ignore any .mcp.json in the repo or MCP servers in user settings. To approve every tool of one server, the allow rule needs the full prefix and a star, such as mcp__playwright__*. A bare mcp__* or * in allowedTools is ignored.

lab.title: A kb_search of your own
needs: For two steps only: your own Anthropic API key
lab.goal: Build an in-process MCP tool, look at it through a real MCP client without any model, test its handler, then let a session call it.

guess.q: Your server is registered as mcpServers: { brain: createSdkMcpServer({ name: "nova", tools: [kbSearch] }) }. Which name must be in allowedTools?

options.why: The name inside createSdkMcpServer is not the one that counts. The key in mcpServers is.
The docs say the key you use in mcpServers becomes the server part of the full tool name.
The model sees the full prefixed name, and allow rules match that full name.

follow.say: Write src/kb.ts from the Understand step. The SDK already installed the MCP library as a peer dependency, so the import works.
Look at your tool through a real MCP client, connected with in-memory pipes, so no model and no network are involved. Create src/mcp-peek.ts:
A handler is an ordinary function, so test it like one. tool() returns an object with the handler on it.
follow.see:
✔ kb_search answers from the right page (0.390208ms)
✔ a question with no page is an error the model can read (0.057542ms)
ℹ tests 2

follow.say: Now let a session use it. Create src/ask-kb.ts from the Understand step and run it with your key.
follow.do:
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...   # your own key
npx tsx src/ask-kb.ts
follow.see: (Needs your key; the wording will differ.) Possibly a ToolSearch call first, then tool call: mcp__nova__kb_search, then denied: [] and an answer saying a lite VM has 4 vCPU, taken from your handler's text.

follow.say: Remove the allowedTools line and run it once more, so you see what dontAsk does with a tool nobody approved.
follow.see: (Needs your key.) The model tries mcp__nova__kb_search, the call appears in denied, and the answer says it could not search.

lab.build: Add a second tool, post_progress, to the nova server. It takes { text: z.string().max(200) } and appends a line with the time and the text to progress.log, then returns the text "posted". Run mcp-peek again to see both tools listed and that a 500-character text is refused before the handler runs. Add a node:test for the length limit, then put the new tool's full name into allowedTools and, with your key, ask the session to search and then post one short update.
checks: mcp-peek lists kb_search with a JSON Schema whose required list is ["question"].
A call with question: 42 is refused with an input validation error, and your handler never runs.
node --test passes for the handler tests without any API key.
With your key, the session prints tool call: mcp__nova__kb_search and an empty denied list.
After your build, mcp-peek lists two tools and progress.log gets one line when the session posts.
lab.fix: A teammate's tool is called search with the description "Search." and an input { q: z.string() }. In ten test runs the model called it only twice, and once it passed a whole paragraph as q. Nothing is wrong with the handler. Find the two parts of the tool the model actually reads, and rewrite them so the model knows when to call it and what to send.
explain: The model never runs your TypeScript. What does it read to decide whether to call your tool, and what does it send?
Where does the server part of mcp__<server>__<tool> come from, and why must the full name be in allowedTools?
What does the model receive when your handler throws, and when would you return isError: true yourself instead?
lab.done: Your tool is visible through an MCP client, its handler is tested, and a session calls it by its full name.

check.q: Two tools do the same job, but the model keeps choosing the other one. What is the first thing to change in yours?

options.text: The name of the TypeScript function that holds the handler
options.why: The model never sees your code. It sees the tool's name, description and schema.

options.text: Its position in the tools array
options.why: Order is not how the model chooses. It matches the task against what each tool says it does.

options.text: The description, written for the model: what the tool does and when to use it
options.why: The description is the real interface. The model decides from those words whether the tool fits the task.

check.q: Your handler throws new Error("kb offline"). What happens?

options.text: The model gets a failed tool result with the text "kb offline" and the session continues
options.why: The in-process server catches the throw and turns it into an error result. The model can retry or explain.
A tool failure is not a session failure. The loop keeps going.

options.text: The SDK retries the handler three times, then stops the session
options.why: There is no automatic retry of your handler. The model decides what to do next.

check.q: You register mcpServers: { slack: createSdkMcpServer({ name: "nova", tools: [askHuman] }) } with permissionMode "dontAsk". Which allowedTools entry lets ask_human run?

options.why: Allow rules match the full prefixed name the model calls.
The name inside createSdkMcpServer does not decide the prefix. The key in mcpServers does.
The key in mcpServers, slack, becomes the server part of the full tool name.

p: nova-worker builds one in-process server called nova with three tools. ask_human posts a question to the ticket's Slack thread and ends the turn, so the run waits for a person without holding a busy VM. post_progress posts a short update. kb_search runs the team's kb search command over a local copy of the R&D brain, so Nova ranks pages the same way people do. Every handler talks to the broker, which holds the Slack, GitHub and Jira tokens; the VM itself holds none.
The QA agent uses an external server: a pinned Playwright MCP program that drives a browser, loaded alone with strictMcpConfig so no repo or user configuration can add other servers.

tickets.why: tools.ts is three tool() calls and one createSdkMcpServer(); every handler goes through the broker.
The QA agent's browser is an external stdio MCP server, allowed with a server-wide rule.

words.plain: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for a program to offer tools, with a name, description and input schema, to a model.
The program that offers the tools and runs the calls. With the SDK it can live inside your own process.
The SDK helper that makes one tool from a name, a description, a zod shape and an async handler.
Your async function that runs when the model calls the tool and returns content blocks.
mcp__<server>__<tool>: the name the model calls and the name allow rules must match.

review.q: Write a tool() call from memory for a tool that adds two numbers.
review.a: tool("add", "Add two numbers and return the sum.", { a: z.number(), b: z.number() }, async ({ a, b }) => ({ content: [{ type: "text", text: String(a + b) }] })).

review.q: Why does Nova's ask_human go through the broker instead of calling Slack directly?
review.a: The VM has no Slack token on purpose. The broker holds it and only posts into the run's own thread, so even a fooled model cannot post anywhere else.

remember: The model only sees a tool's name, description and schema; your handler does the work, and the full name mcp__server__tool must be allowed.
